entries.abe85f96ffe7cbbf937ad920d04ff50bbb514062: <div sID="gen34265" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="21" osisID="Rev.21" sID="Rev.21"/> <div eID="gen34265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34266" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34267" type="x-p"/> Hitherto the prophecy of this book has presented to us a very remarkable mixture of light and shade, prosperity and adversity, mercy and judgment, in the conduct of divine Providence towards the church in the world: now, at the close of all, the day breaks, and the shadows flee away; a new world now appears, the former having passed away. Some are willing to understand all that is said in these last two chapters of the state of the church even here on earth, in the glory of the latter days; but others, more probably, take it as a representation of the perfect and triumphant state of the church in heaven. Let but the faithful saints and servants of God wait awhile, and they shall not only see, but enjoy, the perfect holiness and happiness of that world. In this chapter you have, I. An introduction to the vision of the new Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.1-Rev.21.9">ver. 1-9</reference>. II. The vision itself, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.10-Rev.21.27">ver. 10</reference>, &c.
entries.6f7bcfb656690f613de0c4b9d1b5e522d7109aaf: <div eID="gen34267" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34266" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The New Jerusalem. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 95.)</title> <div sID="gen34268" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And I saw a new heaven and a new earth: for the first heaven and the first earth were passed away; and there was no more sea. <hi type="super">2</hi> And I John saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. <hi type="super">3</hi> And I heard a great voice out of heaven saying, Behold, the tabernacle of God <hi type="italic">is</hi> with men, and he will dwell with them, and they shall be his people, and God himself shall be with them, <hi type="italic">and be</hi> their God. <hi type="super">4</hi> And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away. <hi type="super">5</hi> And he that sat upon the throne said, Behold, I make all things new. And he said unto me, Write: for these words are true and faithful. 6 And he said unto me, It is done. I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end. I will give unto him that is athirst of the fountain of the water of life freely. <hi type="super">7</hi> He that overcometh shall inherit all things; and I will be his God, and he shall be my son. <hi type="super">8</hi> But the fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable, and murderers, and whoremongers, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone: which is the second death. <div eID="gen34268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34269" type="x-p"/> We have here a more general account of the happiness of the church of God in the future state, by which it seems most safe to understand the heavenly state. <div eID="gen34269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34270" type="x-p"/> I. A new world now opens to our view (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">I saw a new heaven and a new earth;</hi> that is, a new universe; for we suppose the world to be made up of heaven and earth. By the new earth we may understand a new state for the bodies of men, as well as a heaven for their souls. This world is not now newly created, but newly opened, and filled with all those who were the heirs of it. The new heaven and the new earth will not then be distinct; the very earth of the saints, their glorified bodies, will now be spiritual and heavenly, and suited to those pure and bright mansions. To make way for the commencement of this new world, the old world, with all its troubles and commotions, <hi type="italic">passed away.</hi> <div eID="gen34270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34271" type="x-p"/> II. In this new world the apostle <hi type="italic">saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down from heaven,</hi> not locally, but as to its original: this new Jerusalem is the church of God in its new and perfect state, <hi type="italic">prepared as a bride adorned for her husband,</hi> beautified with all perfection of wisdom and holiness, meet for the full fruition of the Lord Jesus Christ in glory. <div eID="gen34271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34272" type="x-p"/> III. The blessed presence of God with his people is here proclaimed and admired: <hi type="italic">I heard a great voice out of heaven, saying, Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="Rev.21.3">v. 3</reference>. Observe, 1. The presence of God with his church is the glory of the church. 2. It is matter of wonder that a holy God should ever dwell with any of the children of men. 3. The presence of God with his people in heaven will not be interrupted as it is on earth, but he will dwell with them continually. 4. The covenant, interest, and relation, that there are now between God and his people, will be filled up and perfected in heaven. <hi type="italic">They shall be his people;</hi> their souls shall be assimilated to him, filled with all the love, honour, and delight in God which their relation to him requires, and this will constitute their perfect holiness; and he will be their God: <hi type="italic">God himself will be their God;</hi> his immediate presence with them, his love fully manifested to them, and his glory put upon them, will be their perfect happiness; then he will fully answer the character of the relation on his part, as they shall do on their part. <div eID="gen34272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34273" type="x-p"/> IV. This new and blessed state will be free from all trouble and sorrow; for, 1. All the effects of former trouble shall be done away. They have been often before in tears, by reason of sin, of affliction, of the calamities of the church; but now <hi type="italic">all tears shall be wiped away;</hi> no signs, no remembrance of former sorrows shall remain, any further than to make their present felicity the greater. God himself, as their tender Father, with his own kind hand, <hi type="italic">shall wipe away the tears</hi> of his children; and they would not have been without those tears when God shall come and wipe them away. 2. All the causes of future sorrow shall be for ever removed: <hi type="italic">There shall be neither death nor pain;</hi> and therefore <hi type="italic">no sorrow nor crying;</hi> these are things incident to that state in which they were before, but now all <hi type="italic">former things have passed away.</hi> <div eID="gen34273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34274" type="x-p"/> V. The truth and certainty of this blessed state are ratified by the word and promise of God, and ordered to be committed to writing, as matter of perpetual record, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.5-Rev.21.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. The subject-matter of this vision is so great, and of such great importance to the church and people of God, that they have need of the fullest assurances of it; and God therefore from heaven repeats and ratifies the truth thereof. Besides, many ages must pass between the time when this vision was given forth and the accomplishment of it, and many great trials must intervene; and therefore God would have it committed to writing, for perpetual memory, and continual use to his people. Observe, 1. The certainty of the promise averred: <hi type="italic">These words are faithful and true;</hi> and it follows, <hi type="italic">It is done,</hi> is as sure as if it were done already. We may and ought to take God's promise as present payment; if he has said that he <hi type="italic">makes all things new, it is done.</hi> 2. He gives us his titles of honour as a pledge or surety of the full performance, even those titles of <hi type="italic">Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end.</hi> As it was his glory that he gave the rise and beginning to the world and to his church, it will be his glory to finish the work begin, and not to leave it imperfect. As his power and will were the first cause of all things, his pleasure and glory are the last end, and he will not lose his design; for then he would no longer be the <hi type="italic">Alpha and Omega.</hi> Men may begin designs which they can never bring to perfection; but <hi type="italic">the counsel of God shall stand,</hi> and he will do all his pleasure. 3. The desires of his people towards this blessed state furnish another evidence of the truth and certainty of it. They thirst after a state of sinless perfection and the uninterrupted enjoyment of God, and God has wrought in them these longing desires, which cannot be satisfied with any thing else, and therefore would be the torment of the soul if they were disappointed but it would be inconsistent with the goodness of God, and his love to his people, to create in them holy and heavenly desires, and then deny them their proper satisfaction; and therefore they may be assured that, when they have overcome their present difficulties, <hi type="italic">he will give them of the fountain of the water of life freely.</hi> <div eID="gen34274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34275" type="x-p"/> VI. The greatness of this future felicity is declared and illustrated, 1. By the freeness of it—it is the free gift of God: <hi type="italic">He gives of the water of life freely;</hi> this will not make it less but more grateful to his people. 2. The fulness of it. The people of God then lie at the fountain-head of all blessedness: they <hi type="italic">inherit all things</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.7">v. 7</reference>); enjoying God, they enjoy all things. He is all in all. 3. By the tenure and title by which they enjoy this blessedness—by right of inheritance, as <hi type="italic">the sons of God,</hi> a title of all others the most honourable, as resulting from so near and endeared a relation to God himself, and the most sure and indefeasible, that can no more cease than the relation from which it results. 4. By the vastly different state of the wicked. Their misery helps to illustrate the glory and blessedness of the saints, and the distinguishing goodness of God towards them, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.8">v. 8</reference>. Here observe, (1.) The sins of those who perish, among which are first mentioned their cowardliness and unbelief. <hi type="italic">The fearful</hi> lead the van in this black list. They durst not encounter the difficulties of religion, and their slavish fear proceeded from their unbelief; but those who were so dastardly as not to dare to take up the cross of Christ, and discharge their duty to him, were yet so desperate as to run into all manner of abominable wickedness—<hi type="italic">murder, adultery, sorcery, idolatry,</hi> and <hi type="italic">lying.</hi> (2.) Their punishment: <hi type="italic">They have their part in the lake that burns with fire and brimstone, which is the second death.</hi> [1.] They could not burn at a stake for Christ, but they must burn in hell for sin. [2.] They must die another death after their natural death; the agonies and terrors of the first death will consign them over to the far greater terrors and agonies of eternal death, to die and to be always dying. [3.] This misery will be their proper part and portion, what they have justly deserved, what they have in effect chosen, and what they have prepared themselves for by their sins. Thus the misery of the damned will illustrate the blessedness of those that are saved, and the blessedness of the saved will aggravate the misery of those that are damned.
entries.ed3db45210cd65d4afdeb9294b8d4cc1c0fd7ed7: <div eID="gen34275" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The New Jerusalem. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 95.)</title> <div sID="gen34276" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> And there came unto me one of the seven angels which had the seven vials full of the seven last plagues, and talked with me, saying, Come hither, I will show thee the bride, the Lamb's wife. <hi type="super">10</hi> And he carried me away in the spirit to a great and high mountain, and showed me that great city, the holy Jerusalem, descending out of heaven from God, <hi type="super">11</hi> Having the glory of God: and her light <hi type="italic">was</hi> like unto a stone most precious, even like a jasper stone, clear as crystal; <hi type="super">12</hi> And had a wall great and high, <hi type="italic">and</hi> had twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and names written thereon, which are <hi type="italic">the names</hi> of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel: <hi type="super">13</hi> On the east three gates; on the north three gates; on the south three gates; and on the west three gates. <hi type="super">14</hi> And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and in them the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb. <hi type="super">15</hi> And he that talked with me had a golden reed to measure the city, and the gates thereof, and the wall thereof. <hi type="super">16</hi> And the city lieth foursquare, and the length is as large as the breadth: and he measured the city with the reed, twelve thousand furlongs. The length and the breadth and the height of it are equal. <hi type="super">17</hi> And he measured the wall thereof, a hundred <hi type="italic">and</hi> forty <hi type="italic">and</hi> four cubits, <hi type="italic">according to</hi> the measure of a man, that is, of the angel. 18 And the building of the wall of it was <hi type="italic">of</hi> jasper: and the city <hi type="italic">was</hi> pure gold, like unto clear glass. <hi type="super">19</hi> And the foundations of the wall of the city <hi type="italic">were</hi> garnished with all manner of precious stones. The first foundation <hi type="italic">was</hi> jasper; the second, sapphire; the third, a chalcedony; the fourth, an emerald; <hi type="super">20</hi> The fifth, sardonyx; the sixth, sardius; the seventh, chrysolite; the eighth, beryl; the ninth, a topaz; the tenth, a chrysoprasus; the eleventh, a jacinth; the twelfth, an amethyst. <hi type="super">21</hi> And the twelve gates <hi type="italic">were</hi> twelve pearls; every several gate was of one pearl: and the street of the city <hi type="italic">was</hi> pure gold, as it were transparent glass. <hi type="super">22</hi> And I saw no temple therein: for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of it. <hi type="super">23</hi> And the city had no need of the sun, neither of the moon, to shine in it: for the glory of God did lighten it, and the Lamb <hi type="italic">is</hi> the light thereof. <hi type="super">24</hi> And the nations of them which are saved shall walk in the light of it: and the kings of the earth do bring their glory and honour into it. 25 And the gates of it shall not be shut at all by day: for there shall be no night there. <hi type="super">26</hi> And they shall bring the glory and honour of the nations into it. <hi type="super">27</hi> And there shall in no wise enter into it any thing that defileth, neither <hi type="italic">whatsoever</hi> worketh abomination, or <hi type="italic">maketh</hi> a lie: but they which are written in the Lamb's book of life. <div eID="gen34276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34277" type="x-p"/> We have already considered the introduction to the vision of the new Jerusalem in a more general idea of the heavenly state; we now come to the vision itself, where observe, <div eID="gen34277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34278" type="x-p"/> I. The person that opened the vision to the apostle—<hi type="italic">one of the seven angels, that had the seven vials full of the seven last plagues,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.21.9">v. 9</reference>. God has a variety of work and employment for his holy angels. Sometimes they are to sound the trumpet of divine Providence, and give fair warning to a careless world; sometimes they are to pour out the vials of God's anger upon impenitent sinners; and sometimes to discover things of a heavenly nature to those that are <hi type="italic">the heirs of salvation.</hi> They readily execute every commission they receive from God; and, when this world shall be at an end, yet the angels shall be employed by the great God in proper pleasant work to all eternity. <div eID="gen34278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34279" type="x-p"/> II. The place from which the apostle had this glorious view and prospect. He was taken, in ecstasy, into <hi type="italic">a high mountain.</hi> From such situations men usually have the most distinct views of adjacent cities. Those who would have clear views of heaven must get as near heaven as they can, into the mount of vision, the mount of meditation and faith, whence, as from the top of Pisgah, they may behold the goodly land of the heavenly Canaan. <div eID="gen34279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34280" type="x-p"/> III. The subject-matter of the vision—<hi type="italic">the bride, the Lamb's wife</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.10">v. 10</reference>); that is, the church of God in her glorious, perfect, triumphant state, under the resemblance of Jerusalem, having the glory of God shining in its lustre, as <hi type="italic">uxor splendit radiis mariti—the bride comely through the comeliness put on her by her husband;</hi> glorious in her relation to Christ, in his image now perfected in her, and in his favour shining upon her. And now we have a large description of the church triumphant under the emblem of a city, far exceeding in riches and splendour all the cities of this world; and this new Jerusalem is here represented to us both in the exterior and the interior part of it. <div eID="gen34280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34281" type="x-p"/> 1. The exterior part of the city—<hi type="italic">the wall</hi> and <hi type="italic">the gates,</hi> the wall for security and the gates for entrance. <div eID="gen34281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34282" type="x-p"/> (1.) The wall for security. Heaven is a safe state; those that are there are enclosed with a wall, that separates them and secures them from all evils and enemies: now here, in the account of the wall, we observe, [1.] The height of it, which, we are told, is very high, <hi type="italic">seventy yards</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.17">v. 17</reference>), sufficient both for ornament and security. [2.] The matter of it: <hi type="italic">It was as jasper;</hi> a wall all built of the most precious stones, for firmness and lustre, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.11">v. 11</reference>. This city has a wall that is impregnable as well as precious. [3.] The form of it was very regular and uniform: <hi type="italic">It was four-square, the length as large as the breadth.</hi> In the new Jerusalem all shall be equal in purity and perfection. There shall be an absolute uniformity in the church triumphant, a thing wanted and wished for on earth, but not to be expected till we come to heaven. [4.] The measure of the wall (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.15-Rev.21.16">v. 15, 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">Twelve thousand furlongs</hi> each way, each side, which is forty-eight thousand furlongs in the whole compass, or fifteen hundred German miles. Here is room sufficient for all the people of God—<hi type="italic">many mansions in their Father's house.</hi> [5.] The foundation of the wall, for heaven is a city that hath her foundations (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.19">v. 19</reference>); the promise and power of God, and the purchase of Christ, are the strong foundations of the church's safety and happiness. The foundations are described by their number—<hi type="italic">twelve,</hi> alluding to the twelve apostles (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.14">v. 14</reference>), whose gospel doctrines are the foundations upon which the church is built, <hi type="italic">Christ himself being the chief corner-stone;</hi> and, as to the matter of these foundations, it was various and precious, set forth by twelve sorts of precious stones, denoting the variety and excellency of the doctrines of the gospel, or of the graces of the Holy Spirit, or the personal excellencies of the Lord Jesus Christ. <div eID="gen34282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34283" type="x-p"/> (2.) The gates for entrance. Heaven is not inaccessible; there is a way opened into the holiest of all; there is a free admission to all those that are sanctified; they shall not find themselves shut out. Now, as to these gates, observe, [1.] Their number—<hi type="italic">twelve gates,</hi> answering to the twelve tribes of Israel. All the true Israel of God shall have entrance into the new Jerusalem, as every tribe had into the earthly Jerusalem. [2.] Their guards which were placed upon them—<hi type="italic">twelve angels,</hi> to admit and receive the several tribes of the spiritual Israel and keep out others. [3.] The inscription on the gates—<hi type="italic">the names of the twelve tribes,</hi> to show that they have a right to the tree of life, and to enter through the gates into the city. [4.] The situation of the gates. As the city had four equal sides, answering to the four quarters of the world, east, west, north, and south, so on each side there were three gates, signifying that from all quarters of the earth there shall be some who shall get safely to heaven and be received there, and that there is as free entrance from one part of the world as from the other; <hi type="italic">for in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, Barbarian, Scythian, bond, nor free.</hi> Men of all nations, and languages, who believe on Christ, have by him access to God in grace here and in glory hereafter. [5.] The materials of these gates—they were all of pearls, and yet with great variety: <hi type="italic">Every gate one pearl,</hi> either one single pearl of that vast bigness, or one single sort of pearl. Christ is the pearl of great price, and he is our way to God. There is nothing magnificent enough in this world fully to set forth the glory of heaven. Could we, in the glass of a strong imagination, contemplate such a city as is here described, even as to the exterior part of it, such a wall, and such gates, how amazing, how glorious, would the prospect be! And yet this is but a faint and dim representation of what heaven is in itself. <div eID="gen34283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34284" type="x-p"/> 2. The interior part of the new Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.22-Rev.21.27">v. 22-27</reference>. We have seen its strong wall, and stately gates, and glorious guards; now we are to be led through the gates into the city itself; and the first thing which we observe there is the street of the city, <hi type="italic">which is of pure gold, like transparent glass,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.21.21">v. 21</reference>. The saints in heaven tread upon gold. The new Jerusalem has its several streets. There is the most exact order in heaven: every saint has his proper mansion. There is converse in heaven: the saints are then at rest, but it is not a mere passive rest; it is not a state of sleep and inactivity, but a state of delightful motion: <hi type="italic">The nations that are saved walk in the light of it.</hi> They walk with Christ in white. They have communion not only with God, but with one another; and all their steps are firm and clean. They are pure and clear <hi type="italic">as gold and transparent glass.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen34284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34285" type="x-p"/> (1.) The temple of the new Jerusalem, which was no material temple, made with men's hands, as that of Solomon and Zerubbabel, but a temple altogether spiritual and divine; <hi type="italic">for the Lord God Almighty, and the Lamb, are the temple thereof.</hi> There the saints are above the need of ordinances, which were the means of their preparation for heaven. When the end is attained the means are no longer useful. Perfect and immediate communion with God will more than supply the place of gospel institutions. <div eID="gen34285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34286" type="x-p"/> (2.) The light of this city. Where there is no light, there can be no lustre nor pleasure. Heaven is <hi type="italic">the inheritance of the saints in light.</hi> But what is that light? There is no sun nor moon shining there, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.23">v. 23</reference>. Light is sweet, and a pleasant thing it is to behold the sun. What a dismal world would this be if it were not for the light of the sun! What is there in heaven that supplies the want of it? There is no want of the light of the sun, <hi type="italic">for the glory of God lightens that city, and the Lamb is the light thereof.</hi> God in Christ will be an everlasting fountain of knowledge and joy to the saints in heaven; and, if so, there is no need of the sun or moon, any more than we here need to set up candles at noon day, when the sun shineth in its strength. <div eID="gen34286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34287" type="x-p"/> (3.) The inhabitants of this city. They are described here several ways. [1.] By their numbers—whole nations of saved souls; some out of all nations, and many out of some nations. All those multitudes who were sealed on earth are saved in heaven. [2.] By their dignity—some of the kings and princes of the earth: great kings. God will have some of all ranks and degrees of men to fill the heavenly mansions, high and low; and when the greatest kings come to heaven they will see all their former honour and glory swallowed up of this heavenly glory that so much excels. [3.] Their continual accession and entrance into this city: <hi type="italic">The gates shall never be shut.</hi> There is no night, and therefore no need of shutting up the gates. Some one or other is coming in every hour and moment, and those that are sanctified always find the gates open; they have <hi type="italic">an abundant entrance into the kingdom.</hi> <div eID="gen34287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34288" type="x-p"/> (4.) The accommodations of this city: All the <hi type="italic">glory and honour of the nations shall be brought into it.</hi> Whatever is excellent and valuable in this world shall be there enjoyed in a more refined kind, and to a far greater degree—brighter crowns, a better and more enduring substance, more sweet and satisfying feasts, a more glorious attendance, a truer sense of honour and far higher posts of honour, a more glorious temper of mind, and a form and a countenance more glorious than ever were known in this world. <div eID="gen34288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34289" type="x-p"/> (5.) The unmixed purity of all who belong to the new Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.27">v. 27</reference>. [1.] There the saints shall have no impure thing remaining in them. In the article of death they shall be cleansed from every thing that is of a defiling nature. Now they feel a sad mixture of corruption with their graces, which hinders them in the service of God, interrupts their communion with him, and intercepts the light of his countenance; but, at their entrance into the holy of holies, they are washed in the laver of Christ's blood, and presented to the Father without spot. [2.] There the saints shall have no impure persons admitted among them. In the earthly Jerusalem there will be a mixed communion, after all the care that can be taken. Some roots of bitterness will spring up to trouble and defile Christian societies; but in the new Jerusalem there is a society perfectly pure. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Free from such as are openly profane. There are none admitted into heaven who work abominations. In the churches on earth sometimes abominable things are done, solemn ordinances profaned and prostituted to men openly vicious, for worldly ends; but no such abominations can have place in heaven. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Free from hypocrites, such as make lies, say they are Jews, and are not, but do lie. These will creep into the churches of Christ on earth, and may lie concealed there a long time, perhaps all their days; but they cannot intrude into the new Jerusalem, which is wholly reserved for those that are called, and chosen, and faithful, who are all written, not only in the register if the visible church, <hi type="italic">but in the Lamb's book of life.</hi>  <chapter eID="Rev.21"/> <div eID="gen34289" type="x-p"/>

entries.d4d9ddca45d3a71a84085f55c8285bfd21f9b4aa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19393"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 21</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Rev.21.1-Rev.21.27">Re 21:1-27</reference>. The New Heaven and Earth: New Jerusalem Out of Heaven.</title> <div sID="gen42460" type="x-p"/> The remaining two chapters describe the eternal and consummated kingdom of God and the saints on the new earth. As the world of nations is to be pervaded by divine influence in the millennium, so the world of nature shall be, not annihilated, but transfigured universally in the eternal state which follows it. The earth was cursed for man's sake; but is redeemed by the second Adam. Now is the Church; in the millennium shall be the kingdom; and after that shall be the new world wherein God shall be all in all. The "day of the Lord" and the conflagration of the earth are in <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.10">2Pe 3:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.11">11</reference> spoken of as if connected together, from which many argue against a millennial interval between His coming and the general conflagration of the old earth, preparatory to the new; but "day" is used often of a whole period comprising events intimately connected together, as are the Lord's second advent, the millennium, and the general conflagration and judgment. Compare <reference osisRef="Gen.2.4">Ge 2:4</reference> as to the wide use of "day." Man's soul is redeemed by regeneration through the Holy Spirit now; man's body shall be redeemed at the resurrection; man's dwelling-place, His inheritance, the earth, shall be redeemed perfectly at the creation of the new heaven and earth, which shall exceed in glory the first Paradise, as much as the second Adam exceeds in glory the first Adam before the fall, and as man regenerated in body and soul shall exceed man as he was at creation.<div eID="gen42460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42461" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19393"/><hi type="bold">1. the first--</hi>that is the former.<div eID="gen42461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42462" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">passed away--</hi>Greek, in A and B is "were departed" (Greek, "apeelthon," not as in English Version, "pareelthe").<div eID="gen42462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42463" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was--</hi>Greek, "is," which graphically sets the thing before our eyes as present.<div eID="gen42463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42464" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no more sea--</hi>The sea is the type of perpetual unrest. Hence our Lord rebukes it as an unruly hostile troubler of His people. It symbolized the political tumults out of which "the beast" arose, <reference osisRef="Rev.13.1">Re 13:1</reference>. As the physical corresponds to the spiritual and moral world, so the absence of sea, after the metamorphosis of the earth by fire, answers to the unruffled state of solid peace which shall then prevail. The sea, though severing lands from one another, is now, by God's eliciting of good from evil, made the medium of communication between countries through navigation. Then man shall possess inherent powers which shall make the sea no longer necessary, but an element which would detract from a perfect state. A "river" and "water" are spoken of in <reference osisRef="Rev.22.1">Re 22:1</reference>, 2, probably literal (that is, with such changes of the natural properties of water, as correspond analogically to man's own transfigured body), as well as symbolical. The sea was once the element of the world's destruction, and is still the source of death to thousands, whence after the millennium, at the general judgment, it is specially said, "The sea gave up the dead ... in it." Then it shall cease to destroy, or disturb, being removed altogether on account of its past destructions. <div eID="gen42464" type="x-p"/>
entries.2e8f78239ae633253c2b2be0956f00378b5dd6a2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19394"/><div sID="gen42465" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19394"/><hi type="bold">2. And I John--</hi>"John" is omitted in A, B, Vulgate, Syriac, Coptic, and Andreas; also the "I" in the Greek of these authorities is not emphatic. The insertion of "I John" in the Greek would somewhat interfere with the close connection which subsists between "the new heaven and earth," <reference osisRef="Rev.21.1">Re 21:1</reference>, and the "new Jerusalem" in this verse.<div eID="gen42465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42466" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jerusalem ... out of heaven--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rev.3.12">Re 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.4.26">Ga 4:26</reference>, "Jerusalem which is above"; <reference osisRef="Heb.11.10">He 11:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.22">12:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.13.14">13:14</reference>). The descent of the new Jerusalem out of heaven is plainly distinct from the earthly Jerusalem in which Israel in the flesh shall dwell during the millennium, and follows on the creation of the new heaven and earth. John in his Gospel always writes [Greek] Hierosoluma of the old city; in the Apocalypse always Hierousaleem of the heavenly city (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.12">Re 3:12</reference>). Hierousaleem is a Hebrew name, the original and holy appellation. Hierosoluma is the common Greek term, used in a political sense. Paul observes the same distinction when refuting Judaism (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.26">Ga 4:26</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Gal.1.17">Ga 1:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.18">18</reference>; 2:1; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.22">He 12:22</reference>), though not so in the Epistles to Romans and Corinthians [Bengel].<div eID="gen42466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42467" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bride--</hi>made up of the blessed citizens of "the holy city." There is no longer merely a Paradise as in Eden (though there is that also, <reference osisRef="Rev.2.7">Re 2:7</reference>), no longer a mere garden, but now the city of God on earth, costlier, statelier, and more glorious, but at the same time the result of labor and pains such as had not to be expended by man in dressing the primitive garden of Eden. "The lively stones" were severally in time laboriously chiselled into shape, after the pattern of "the Chief corner-stone," to prepare them for the place which they shall everlastingly fill in the heavenly Jerusalem. <div eID="gen42467" type="x-p"/>
entries.6a07ab778957851b72553bfc87616dec44887c6f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19395"/><div sID="gen42468" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19395"/><hi type="bold">3. out of heaven--</hi>so Andreas. But A and Vulgate read, "out of the throne."<div eID="gen42468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42469" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the tabernacle--</hi>alluding to the tabernacle of God in the wilderness (wherein many signs of His presence were given): of which this is the antitype, having previously been in heaven: <reference osisRef="Rev.11.19">Re 11:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.15.5">15:5</reference>, "the temple of the tabernacle of the testimony in heaven"; also <reference osisRef="Rev.13.6">Re 13:6</reference>. Compare the contrast in <reference osisRef="Heb.9.23">He 9:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.14">14</reference>, between "the patterns" and "the heavenly things themselves," between "the figures" and "the true." The earnest of the true and heavenly tabernacle was afforded in the Jerusalem temple described in Eze 40:1-42:20, as about to be, namely, during the millennium.<div eID="gen42469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42470" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dwell with them--</hi>literally, "tabernacle with them"; the same Greek word as is used of the divine Son "tabernacling among us." Then He was in the weakness of the flesh: but at the new creation of heaven and earth He shall tabernacle among us in the glory of His manifested Godhead (<reference osisRef="Rev.22.4">Re 22:4</reference>).<div eID="gen42470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42471" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they--</hi>in Greek emphatic, "they" (in particular).<div eID="gen42471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42472" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his people--</hi>Greek, "His peoples": "the nations of the saved" being all peculiarly His, as Israel was designed to be. So A reads. But B, Vulgate, Syriac, and Coptic read, "His people": singular.<div eID="gen42472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42473" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God himself ... with them--</hi>realizing fully His name Immanuel. <div eID="gen42473" type="x-p"/>
entries.ed9e0b199b35078637ced8084c9eb46362eb87c6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19396"/><div sID="gen42474" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19396"/><hi type="bold">4. all tears--</hi>Greek, "every tear."<div eID="gen42474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42475" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no more death--</hi>Greek, "death shall be no more." Therefore it is not the millennium, for in the latter there is death (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.20">Is 65:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.26">1Co 15:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.54">54</reference>, "the last enemy ... destroyed is death," <reference osisRef="Rev.20.14">Re 20:14</reference>, after the millennium).<div eID="gen42475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42476" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sorrow--</hi>Greek, "mourning."<div eID="gen42476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42477" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">passed away--</hi>Greek, "departed," as in <reference osisRef="Rev.21.1">Re 21:1</reference>. <div eID="gen42477" type="x-p"/>
entries.6ad341e33bbcfeee42e29b071fe0203ab8ce684a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19397"/><div sID="gen42478" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19397"/><hi type="bold">5. sat--</hi>Greek, "sitteth."<div eID="gen42478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42479" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all things new--</hi>not recent, but changed from the old (Greek, "kaina," not "nea"). An earnest of this regeneration and transfiguration of nature is given already in the regenerate soul.<div eID="gen42479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42480" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto me--</hi>so Coptic and Andreas. But A, B, Vulgate, and Syriac omit.<div eID="gen42480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42481" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">true and faithful--</hi>so Andreas. But A, B, Vulgate, Syriac, and Coptic transpose, "faithful and true" (literally, "genuine"). <div eID="gen42481" type="x-p"/>
entries.c318fa28012e4f71f63c4ffb8e73277507f8e57e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19398"/><div sID="gen42482" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19398"/><hi type="bold">6. It is done--</hi>the same Greek as in <reference osisRef="Rev.16.17">Re 16:17</reference>. "It is come to pass." So Vulgate reads with English Version. But A reads, "They ('these words,' <reference osisRef="Rev.21.5">Re 21:5</reference>) are come to pass." All is as sure as if it actually had been fulfilled for it rests on the word of the unchanging God. When the consummation shall be, God shall rejoice over the work of His own hands, as at the completion of the first creation God saw everything that He had made, and behold it was very good (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.31">Ge 1:31</reference>).<div eID="gen42482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42483" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Alpha ... Omega--</hi>Greek in A and B, "the Alpha ... the Omega" (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.18">Re 1:18</reference>).<div eID="gen42483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42484" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">give unto ... athirst ... water of life--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rev.22.17">Re 22:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.12.3">Is 12:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.55.1">55:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.4.13">Joh 4:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.4.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.7.37">7:37</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.7.38">38</reference>). This is added lest any should despair of attaining to this exceeding weight of glory. In our present state we may drink of the stream, then we shall drink at the Fountain.<div eID="gen42484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42485" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">freely--</hi>Greek, "gratuitously": the same Greek as is translated, "(They hated Me) without a cause," <reference osisRef="John.15.25">Joh 15:25</reference>. As gratuitous as was man's hatred of God, so gratuitous is God's love to man: there was every cause in Christ why man should love Him, yet man hated Him; there was every cause in man why (humanly speaking) God should have hated man, yet God loved man: the very reverse of what might be expected took place in both cases. Even in heaven our drinking at the Fountain shall be God's gratuitous gift. <div eID="gen42485" type="x-p"/>
entries.2a5223847e68d6c4d251a34d8eed6da9bb01d84d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19399"/><div sID="gen42486" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19399"/><hi type="bold">7. He that overcometh--</hi>another aspect of the believer's life: a conflict with sin, Satan, and the world is needed. Thirsting for salvation is the first beginning of, and continues for ever (in the sense of an appetite and relish for divine joys) a characteristic of the believer. In a different sense, the believer "shall never thirst."<div eID="gen42486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42487" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">inherit all things--</hi>A, B, Vulgate, and Cyprian read, "these things," namely, the blessings described in this whole passage. With "all things," compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.21-1Cor.3.23">1Co 3:21-23</reference>.<div eID="gen42487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42488" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will be his God--</hi>Greek, "I will be to him a God," that is, all that is implied of blessing in the name "God."<div eID="gen42488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42489" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he shall be my son--</hi>"He" is emphatic: He in particular and in a peculiar sense, above others: Greek, "shall be to me a son," in fullest realization of the promise made in type to Solomon, son of David, and antitypically to the divine Son of David. <div eID="gen42489" type="x-p"/>
entries.76a269df9c994fe085b0734cff4706d66f5fcfa3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19400"/><div sID="gen42490" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19400"/><hi type="bold">8. the fearful--</hi>Greek, "the cowardly," who do not quit themselves like men so as to "overcome" in the good fight; who have the spirit of slavish "fear," not love, towards God; and who through fear of man are not bold for God, or "draw back." Compare <reference osisRef="Rev.21.27">Re 21:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.22.15">22:15</reference>.<div eID="gen42490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42491" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unbelieving--</hi>Greek, "faithless."<div eID="gen42491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42492" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abominable--</hi>who have drank of the harlot's "cup of abominations."<div eID="gen42492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42493" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sorcerers--</hi>one of the characteristics of Antichrist's time.<div eID="gen42493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42494" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all liars--</hi>Greek, "all the liars": or else "all who are liars"; compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.1">1Ti 4:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.2">2</reference>, where similarly lying and dealings with spirits and demons, are joined together as features of "the latter times."<div eID="gen42494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42495" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">second death--</hi><reference osisRef="Rev.20.14">Re 20:14</reference>: "everlasting destruction," <reference osisRef="2Thess.1.9">2Th 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.9.44">Mr 9:44</reference>, 46, 48, "Where THEIR worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched." <div eID="gen42495" type="x-p"/>
entries.533d3fc5ea728ae1d31431c1428fa9624b0e527d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19401"/><div sID="gen42496" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19401"/>9. The same angel who had shown John Babylon the harlot, is appropriately employed to show him in contrast new Jerusalem, the Bride (<reference osisRef="Rev.17.1-Rev.17.5">Re 17:1-5</reference>). The angel so employed is the one that had the last seven plagues, to show that the ultimate blessedness of the Church is one end of the divine judgments on her foes.<div eID="gen42496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42497" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto me--</hi>A, B, and Vulgate omit.<div eID="gen42497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42498" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Lamb's wife--</hi>in contrast to her who sat on many waters (<reference osisRef="Rev.17.1">Re 17:1</reference>), (that is, intrigued with many peoples and nations of the world, instead of giving her undivided affections, as the Bride does, to the Lamb. <div eID="gen42498" type="x-p"/>
entries.2e904a72ab67427396d4603c9161de6e11134842: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19402"/><div sID="gen42499" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19402"/>10. The words correspond to <reference osisRef="Rev.17.3">Re 17:3</reference>, to heighten the contrast of the bride and harlot.<div eID="gen42499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42500" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mountain--</hi>Compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.2">Eze 40:2</reference>, where a similar vision is given from a high mountain.<div eID="gen42500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42501" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that great--</hi>omitted in A, B, Vulgate, Syriac, Coptic, and Cyprian. Translate then, "the holy city Jerusalem."<div eID="gen42501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42502" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">descending--</hi>Even in the millennium the earth will not be a suitable abode for transfigured saints, who therefore shall then reign in heaven over the earth. But after the renewal of the earth at the close of the millennium and judgment, they shall descend from heaven to dwell on an earth assimilated to heaven itself. "From God" implies that "we (the city) are God's workmanship." <div eID="gen42502" type="x-p"/>
entries.6420ffb5bc109b69a579704aaaa53b1e3cea6ef0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19403"/><div sID="gen42503" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19403"/><hi type="bold">11. Having the glory of God--</hi>not merely the Shekinah-cloud, but God Himself as her glory dwelling in the midst of her. Compare the type, the earthly Jerusalem in the millennium (<reference osisRef="Zech.2.5">Zec 2:5</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Rev.21.23">Re 21:23</reference>, below).<div eID="gen42503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42504" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">her light--</hi>Greek, "light-giver": properly applied to the heavenly luminaries which diffuse light. Compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Phil.2.15">Php 2:15</reference>, the only other passage where it occurs. The "and" before "her light' is omitted in A, B, and Vulgate.<div eID="gen42504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42505" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">even like--</hi>Greek, "as it were."<div eID="gen42505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42506" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">jasper--</hi>representing watery crystalline brightness. <div eID="gen42506" type="x-p"/>
entries.078be5eb9cf0473132f3c7c268fff449ac6ea852: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19404"/><div sID="gen42507" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19404"/><hi type="bold">12. And--</hi>A and B omit. <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.30-Ezek.48.35">Eze 48:30-35</reference>, has a similar description, which implies that the millennial Jerusalem shall have its exact antitype in the heavenly Jerusalem which shall descend on the finally regenerated earth.<div eID="gen42507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42508" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wall great and high--</hi>setting forth the security of the Church. Also, the exclusion of the ungodly.<div eID="gen42508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42509" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">twelve angels--</hi>guards of the twelve gates: an additional emblem of perfect security, while the gates being never shut (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.25">Re 21:25</reference>) imply perfect liberty and peace. Also, angels shall be the brethren of the heavenly citizens.<div eID="gen42509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42510" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">names of ... twelve tribes--</hi>The inscription of the names on the gates implies that none but the spiritual Israel, God's elect, shall enter the heavenly city. As the millennium wherein literal Israel in the flesh shall be the mother Church, is the antitype to the Old Testament earthly theocracy in the Holy Land, so the heavenly new Jerusalem is the consummation antitypical to the spiritual Israel, the elect Church of Jews and Gentiles being now gathered out: as the spiritual Israel now is an advance upon the previous literal and carnal Israel, so the heavenly Jerusalem shall be much in advance of the millennial Jerusalem. <div eID="gen42510" type="x-p"/>
entries.86ef2195ab36f1c5addba12517a297bfbb9cb04a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19405"/><div sID="gen42511" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19405"/><hi type="bold">13. On the north ... on the south--</hi>A, B, Vulgate, Syriac, and Coptic read, "And on the north and on the south." In Ezekiel, Joseph, Benjamin, Dan (for which Manasseh is substituted in <reference osisRef="Rev.7.6">Re 7:6</reference>), are on the east (<reference osisRef="Ezek.48.32">Eze 48:32</reference>); Reuben, Judah, Levi, are on the north (<reference osisRef="Ezek.48.31">Eze 48:31</reference>); Simeon, Issachar, Zebulun, on the south (<reference osisRef="Ezek.48.33">Eze 48:33</reference>); Gad, Asher, Naphtali, on the west (<reference osisRef="Ezek.48.34">Eze 48:34</reference>). In Numbers, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun are on the east (<reference osisRef="Num.2.3">Nu 2:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.7">5, 7</reference>). Reuben, Simeon, Gad, on the south (<reference osisRef="Num.2.10">Nu 2:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.14">12, 14</reference>). Ephraim, Manasseh, Benjamin, on the west (<reference osisRef="Num.2.18">Nu 2:18</reference>, 20, 22). Dan, Asher, Naphtali, on the north (<reference osisRef="Num.2.25">Nu 2:25</reference>, 27, 29). <div eID="gen42511" type="x-p"/>
entries.7628fcbeb7d05914f383d218edebc954f4ca313c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19406"/><div sID="gen42512" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19406"/><hi type="bold">14. twelve foundations--</hi>Joshua, the type of Jesus, chose twelve men out of the people, to carry twelve stones over the Jordan with them, as Jesus chose twelve apostles to be the twelve foundations of the heavenly city, of which He is Himself the Chief corner-stone. Peter is not the only apostolic rock on whose preaching Christ builds His Church. Christ Himself is the true foundation: the twelve are foundations only in regard to their apostolic testimony concerning Him. Though Paul was an apostle besides the twelve, yet the mystical number is retained, twelve representing the Church, namely thirty the divine number, multiplied by four, the world number.<div eID="gen42512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42513" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in them the names, &c.--</hi>As architects often have their names inscribed on their great works, so the names of the apostles shall be held in everlasting remembrance. Vulgate reads, "in them." But A, B, Syriac, Coptic, and Andreas read, "upon them." These authorities also insert "twelve" before "names." <div eID="gen42513" type="x-p"/>
entries.31fda37666e4b52f869d3680b5a91d7f0973f828: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19407"/><div sID="gen42514" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19407"/><hi type="bold">15. had a golden reed--</hi>so Coptic. But A, B, Vulgate, and Syriac read, "had (as) a measure, a golden reed." In <reference osisRef="Rev.11.2">Re 11:2</reference> the non-measuring of the outer courts of the temple implied its being given up to secular and heathen desecration. So here, on the contrary, the city being measured implies the entire consecration of every part, all things being brought up to the most exact standard of God's holy requirements, and also God's accurate guardianship henceforth of even the most minute parts of His holy city from all evil. <div eID="gen42514" type="x-p"/>
entries.a3db4099dc323772126d71e4858eec772ae0d794: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19408"/><div sID="gen42515" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19408"/><hi type="bold">16. twelve thousand furlongs--</hi>literally, "to twelve thousand stadii": one thousand furlongs being the space between the several twelve gates. Bengel makes the length of each side of the city to be twelve thousand stadii. The stupendous height, length, and breadth being exactly alike, imply its faultless symmetry, transcending in glory all our most glowing conceptions. <div eID="gen42515" type="x-p"/>
entries.37aa42f81084b57ceefbd8d9583bee2246b6acd0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19409"/><div sID="gen42516" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19409"/><hi type="bold">17. hundred ... forty ... four cubits--</hi>twelve times twelve: the Church-number squared. The wall is far beneath the height of the city.<div eID="gen42516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42517" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">measure of a man, that is, of the angel--</hi>The ordinary measure used by men is the measure here used by the angel, distinct from "the measure of the sanctuary." Men shall then be equal to the angels. <div eID="gen42517" type="x-p"/>
entries.5593a2262a169cd8ea1d1c442f8db30d61b97fb5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19410"/><div sID="gen42518" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19410"/><hi type="bold">18. the building--</hi>"the structure" [Tregelles], Greek, "endomeesis."<div eID="gen42518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42519" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gold, like ... clear glass--</hi>Ideal gold, transparent as no gold here is [Alford]. Excellencies will be combined in the heavenly city which now seem incompatible. <div eID="gen42519" type="x-p"/>
entries.f0c07356185de8f7ccb01cf9b7db9a42d825b4ac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19411"/><div sID="gen42520" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19411"/><hi type="bold">19. And--</hi>so Syriac, Coptic, and Andreas. But A, B, and Vulgate omit. Compare <reference osisRef="Rev.21.14">Re 21:14</reference> with this verse; also <reference osisRef="Isa.54.11">Is 54:11</reference>.<div eID="gen42520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42521" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all manner of precious stones--</hi>Contrast <reference osisRef="Rev.18.12">Re 18:12</reference> as to the harlot, Babylon. These precious stones constituted the "foundations."<div eID="gen42521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42522" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chalcedony--</hi>agate from Chalcedon: semi-opaque, sky-blue, with stripes of other colors [Alford]. <div eID="gen42522" type="x-p"/>
entries.10e3f4b64fbd839c5b2371c4cf167c81ede16f82: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19412"/><div sID="gen42523" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19412"/><hi type="bold">20. sardonyx--</hi>a gem having the redness of the cornelian, and the whiteness of the onyx.<div eID="gen42523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42524" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sardius--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Rev.4.3">Re 4:3</reference>).<div eID="gen42524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42525" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chrysolite--</hi>described by Pliny as transparent and of a golden brightness, like our topaz: different from our pale green crystallized chrysolite.<div eID="gen42525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42526" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">beryl--</hi>of a sea-green color.<div eID="gen42526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42527" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">topaz--</hi>Pliny [37.32], makes it green and transparent, like our chrysolite.<div eID="gen42527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42528" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chrysoprasus--</hi>somewhat pale, and having the purple color of the amethyst [Pliny, 37, 20, 21].<div eID="gen42528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42529" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">jacinth--</hi>The flashing violet brightness in the amethyst is diluted in the jacinth [Pliny, 37.41]. <div eID="gen42529" type="x-p"/>
entries.cf97e79dfcc35ecac225ee768278b055db95c0d8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19413"/><div sID="gen42530" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19413"/><hi type="bold">21. every several--</hi>Greek, "each one severally." <div eID="gen42530" type="x-p"/>
entries.7feda3f3098dc7d06211b4200aa2c685dc1aa54e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19414"/><div sID="gen42531" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19414"/><hi type="bold">22. no temple ... God ... the temple--</hi>As God now dwells in the spiritual Church, His "temple" (Greek, "naos," "shrine"; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.17">1Co 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.19">6:19</reference>), so the Church when perfected shall dwell in Him as her "temple" (naos: the same Greek). As the Church was "His sanctuary," so He is to be their sanctuary. Means of grace shall cease when the end of grace is come. Church ordinances shall give place to the God of ordinances. Uninterrupted, immediate, direct, communion with Him and the Lamb (compare <reference osisRef="John.4.23">Joh 4:23</reference>), shall supersede intervening ordinances. <div eID="gen42531" type="x-p"/>
entries.443568cf0d008d17be494c52d6ebf5df03a78352: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19415"/><div sID="gen42532" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19415"/><hi type="bold">23. in it--</hi>so Vulgate. But A, B, and Andreas read, "(shine) on it," or literally, "for her."<div eID="gen42532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42533" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the light--</hi>Greek, "the lamp" (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.19">Is 60:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.60.20">20</reference>). The direct light of God and the Lamb shall make the saints independent of God's creatures, the sun and moon, for light. <div eID="gen42533" type="x-p"/>
entries.b71311ce4c020e934f7808bed9455621fab33621: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19416"/><div sID="gen42534" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19416"/><hi type="bold">24. of them which are saved ... in--</hi>A, B, Vulgate, Coptic, and Andreas read "(the nations shall walk) by means of her light": omitting "of them which are saved." Her brightness shall supply them with light.<div eID="gen42534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42535" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the kings of the earth--</hi>who once had regard only to their glory, having been converted, now in the new Jerusalem do bring their glory into it, to lay it down at the feet of their God and Lord.<div eID="gen42535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42536" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and honour--</hi>so B, Vulgate, and Syriac. But A omits the clause. <div eID="gen42536" type="x-p"/>
entries.44f736e3be5bcc43a4bdcc886697ebb0ea217630: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19417"/><div sID="gen42537" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19417"/><hi type="bold">25. not be shut ... by day--</hi>therefore shall never be shut: for it shall always be day. Gates are usually shut by night: but in it shall be no night. There shall be continual free ingress into it, so as that all which is blessed and glorious may continually be brought into it. So in the millennial type. <div eID="gen42537" type="x-p"/>
entries.ea967bd140779b82b0fd9dd14d48ff20f562914a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19418"/><div sID="gen42538" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19418"/>26. All that was truly glorious and excellent in the earth and its converted nations shall be gathered into it; and while all shall form one Bride, there shall be various orders among the redeemed, analogous to the divisions of nations on earth constituting the one great human family, and to the various orders of angels. <div eID="gen42538" type="x-p"/>
entries.d9f2cc8d678a83818d5a20bda0d68fe4c9b4ef7b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19419"/><div sID="gen42539" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19419"/><hi type="bold">27. anything that defileth--</hi>Greek, "koinoun." A and B read [koinon,] "anything unclean."<div eID="gen42539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42540" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the Lamb's book of life--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Rev.20.12">Re 20:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.20.15">Re 20:15</reference>). As all the filth of the old Jerusalem was carried outside the walls and burnt there, so nothing defiled shall enter the heavenly city, but be burnt outside (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.22.15">Re 22:15</reference>). It is striking that the apostle of love, who shows us the glories of the heavenly city, is he also who speaks most plainly of the terrors of hell. On <reference osisRef="Rev.21.26">Re 21:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.27">27</reference>, Alford writes a Note, rash in speculation, about the heathen nations, above what is written, and not at all required by the sacred text: compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Rev.21.26">Re 21:26</reference>. <chapter eID="Rev.21"/>

entries.95d4635a3d11312a3eb72e674d5732920f5de002: <div eID="gen56757" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen56758" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen56759" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen56759" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen56758" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen56760" type="x-p"/> The new heaven and the new earth, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.1">Rev 21:1</reference>. The new Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.2">Rev 21:2</reference>. God dwells with men; the happy state of his followers, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.3-Rev.21.7">Rev 21:3-7</reference>. The wretched state of the ungodly, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.8">Rev 21:8</reference>. An angel shows John the holy city, the New Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.9">Rev 21:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.10">Rev 21:10</reference>. Her light, wall, gates, and foundations, described, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.11-Rev.21.21">Rev 21:11-21</reference>. God and the Lamb are the temple and light of it, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.22">Rev 21:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.23">Rev 21:23</reference>. The nations and kings of the earth bring their glory and honor to it; the gates shall never be shut, nor shall any defilement enter into it, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.24-Rev.21.27">Rev 21:24-27</reference>. <div eID="gen56760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56761" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen56761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56762" type="x-p"/> A new heaven and a new earth - See the notes on <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.13">2Pet 3:13</reference> : The ancient Jews believed that God would renew the heavens and the earth at the end of seven thousand years. The general supposition they founded on <reference osisRef="Isa.65.17">Isa 65:17</reference>. <div eID="gen56762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56763" type="x-p"/> There was no more sea - The sea no more appeared than did the first heaven and earth. All was made new; and probably the new sea occupied a different position and was differently distributed, from that of the old sea. <div eID="gen56763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56764" type="x-p"/> However, with respect to these subjects as they stand in this most figurative book, I must express myself in the words of Calmet: Vouloir dire quels seront ce nouveau ciel, et cette nouvelle terre, quels seront leurs ornamens et leur qualite, c'est a mon avis la plus grande de toutes les presomptions. En general, ces manieres de parler marquent de tres grands changemens dans l'univers. "To pretend to say what is meant by this new heaven and new earth, and what are their ornaments and qualities, is in my opinion the greatest of all presumptions. In general these figures of speech point out great alternations in the universe."
entries.a018b43e00fd4ade7957d911540cce0978f579d7: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen56764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56765" type="x-p"/> And I John - The writer of this book; whether the evangelist and apostle, or John the Ephesian presbyter, has been long doubted in the Church. <div eID="gen56765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56766" type="x-p"/> New Jerusalem - See the notes on <reference osisRef="Gal.4.24-Gal.4.27">Gal 4:24-27</reference> (note). This doubtless means the Christian Church in a state of great prosperity and purity; but some think eternal blessedness is intended. <div eID="gen56766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56767" type="x-p"/> Coming down from God - It is a maxim of the ancient Jews that both the tabernacle, and the temple, and Jerusalem itself, came down from heaven. And in Midrash Hanaalem, Sohar Gen. fol. 69, col. 271, Rab. Jeremias said, "The holy blessed God shall renew the world, and build Jerusalem, and shall cause it to descend from heaven." Their opinion is, that there is a spiritual temple, a spiritual tabernacle, and a spiritual Jerusalem; and that none of these can be destroyed, because they subsist in their spiritual representatives. See Schoettgen.
entries.299e050e282a35446c699456c86e229dcef36e8b: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen56767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56768" type="x-p"/> The tabernacle of God is with men - God, in the most especial manner, dwells among his followers, diffusing his light and life everywhere.
entries.357a72ba415edc71b15947a18cea8d2ff84e2ccd: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen56768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56769" type="x-p"/> There shall be no more death - Because there shall be a general resurrection. And this is the inference which St Paul makes from his doctrine of a general resurrection, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.26">1Cor 15:26</reference>, where he says, "The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death." But death cannot be destroyed by there being simply no farther death; death can only be destroyed and annihilated by a general resurrection; if there be no general resurrection, it is most evident that death will still retain his empire. Therefore, the fact that there shall be no more death assures the fact that there shall be a general resurrection; and this also is a proof that, after the resurrection, there shall be no more death. See the whole of the note on <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.27">1Cor 15:27</reference>.
entries.578457f1e860f31d53170b3bdae375563171ab0d: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen56769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56770" type="x-p"/> Behold, I make all things new - As the creation of the world at the beginning was the work of God alone, so this new creation. <div eID="gen56770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56771" type="x-p"/> These words are true and faithful - Truth refers to the promise of these changes; faithfulness, to the fulfillment of these promises.
entries.138fe3ef20b05951f791fde32153b6a6b8a8b0f0: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen56771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56772" type="x-p"/> It is done - All is determined, and shall be fulfilled in due time. The great drama is finished, and what was intended is now completed; referring to the period alluded to by the angel. <div eID="gen56772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56773" type="x-p"/> I am Alpha and Omega - See on <reference osisRef="Rev.1.8">Rev 1:8</reference> (note). <div eID="gen56773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56774" type="x-p"/> The fountain of the water of life - See on <reference osisRef="Joh.4.10">Joh 4:10</reference> (note), <reference osisRef="Joh.4.14">Joh 4:14</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Joh.7.37">Joh 7:37</reference> (note), etc. <div eID="gen56774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56775" type="x-p"/> The rabbins consider the fountain of the world to come as one of the particular blessings of a future state. In Sanhedrim, Aboth R. Nathan, c. 31, it is said, "He will show them the excellency of the fountain of the future world, that they may accurately see and consider, and say, Wo to us! what good have we lost! and our race is cut off from the face of the earth."
entries.47678045f117e1621a461c72347208fd1831b1ae: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen56775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56776" type="x-p"/> Inherit all things - Here he had no inheritance; there he shall inherit the kingdom of heaven, and be with God and Christ, and have every possible degree of blessedness.
entries.335150f63e8a83454c5320c9cd64999c6f13065a: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen56776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56777" type="x-p"/> But the fearful - Δειλοις· Those who, for fear of losing life or their property, either refused to receive the Christian religion, though convinced of its truth and importance; or, having received it, in times of persecution fell away, not being willing to risk their lives. <div eID="gen56777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56778" type="x-p"/> And unbelieving - Those who resist against full evidence. And sinners, και ἁμαρτωλοις, is added here by about thirty excellent MSS., and is found in the Syrian, Arabic, some of the Slavonic, and in Andreas and Arethas. On this evidence Griesbach has admitted it into the text. <div eID="gen56778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56779" type="x-p"/> The abominable - Εβδελυγμενοις· Those who are polluted with unnatural lust. <div eID="gen56779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56780" type="x-p"/> And murderers - Φονευσι· Those who take away the life of man for any cause but the murder of another, and those who hate a brother in their heart. <div eID="gen56780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56781" type="x-p"/> And whoremongers - Πορνοις· Adulterers, fornicators, whores, prostitutes, and rakes of every description. <div eID="gen56781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56782" type="x-p"/> Sorcerers - Φαρμακοις· Persons who, by drugs, philtres, fumigations, etc., pretend to produce supernatural effects, chiefly by spiritual agency. <div eID="gen56782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56783" type="x-p"/> Idolaters - Ειδωλολατραις· Those who offer any kind of worship or religious reverence to any thing but God. All image worshippers are idolaters in every sense of the word. <div eID="gen56783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56784" type="x-p"/> And all liars - Και πασι τοις ψευδεσι· Every one who speaks contrary to the truth when he knows the truth, and even he who speaks the truth with the intention to deceive; i.e., to persuade a person that a thing is different from what it really is, by telling only a part of the truth, or suppressing some circumstance which would have led the hearer to a different end to the true conclusion. All these shall have their portion, το μερος, their share, what belongs to them, their right, in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone. This is the second death, from which there is no recovery.
entries.466f98b12d9f75fb6dc42547a564ee3e73f0298d: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen56784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56785" type="x-p"/> The bride, the Lamb's wife - The pure and holy Christian Church.
entries.db2d0afd5a61750cd88382fdf1c0a78ea9014b4d: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen56785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56786" type="x-p"/> To a great and high mountain - That, being above this city, he might see every street and lane of it. <div eID="gen56786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56787" type="x-p"/> The holy Jerusalem - See on <reference osisRef="Rev.21.2">Rev 21:2</reference> (note).
entries.42705f148e627e1cccb99af33efa5bd02f1be413: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen56787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56788" type="x-p"/> Having the glory of God - Instead of the sun and moon, it has the splendor of God to enlighten it. <div eID="gen56788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56789" type="x-p"/> Unto a stone most precious, even like a jasper stone, clear as crystal - Among precious stones there are some even of the same species more valuable than others: for their value is in proportion to their being free from flaws, and of a good water, i.e., a uniform and brilliant transparency. A crystal is perfectly clear, the oriental jasper is a beautiful sea-green. The stone that is here described is represented as a perfectly transparent jasper, being as unclouded as the brightest crystal, and consequently the most precious of its species. Nothing can be finer than this description: the light of this city is ever intense, equal, and splendid; but it is tinged with this green hue, in order to make it agreeable to the sight. Nothing is so friendly to the eye as blue or green; all other colors fatigue; and, if very intense, injure the eye. These are the colors of the earth and sky, on which the eye of man is to be constantly fixed. To these colors the structure of the eye is adapted; and the general appearance of the earth and the sky is adapted to this structure.
entries.7f5e4a327e714514f3fe01a50b76c37ac8255927: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen56789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56790" type="x-p"/> Had a wall great and high - An almighty defense. <div eID="gen56790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56791" type="x-p"/> Twelve gates - A gate for every tribe of Israel, in the vicinity of which gate that tribe dwelt; so that in coming in and going out they did not mix with each other. This description of the city is partly taken from <reference osisRef="Eze.48.30-Eze.48.35">Eze 48:30-35</reference>. <div eID="gen56791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56792" type="x-p"/> In Synopsis Sohar, p. 115, n. 27, it is said: "In the palace of the world to come there are twelve gates, each of which is inscribed with one of the twelve tribes, as that of Reuben, of Simeon, etc.: he, therefore, who is of the tribe of Reuben is received into none of the twelve gates but his own; and so of the rest."
entries.df1dbe07733500b054bf83b63f2f9cae45c948ca: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen56792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56793" type="x-p"/> On the east three gates - The city is here represented as standing to the four cardinal points of heaven, and presenting one side to each of these points.
entries.f6a7d9eea480e15c179c4736a668ae4b031710d7: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen56793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56794" type="x-p"/> The wall - had twelve foundations - Probably twelve stones, one of which served for a foundation or threshold to each gate; and on these were inscribed the names of the twelve apostles, to intimate that it was by the doctrine of the apostles that souls enter into the Church, and thence into the New Jerusalem.
entries.01a4199f677466aea46f339b89ba38bda64a691f: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen56794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56795" type="x-p"/> Had a golden reed - Several excellent MSS. add μετρον, a measure; he had a measuring rod made of gold. This account of measuring the city seems to be copied, with variations, from <reference osisRef="Eze.40.3">Eze 40:3</reference>, etc.
entries.0ac981c41b004c8a48560dff1c1ec3a364ef20a6: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen56795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56796" type="x-p"/> The city lieth foursquare - Each side was equal, consequently the length and breadth were equal; and its height is here said to be equal to its length. It is hard to say how this should be understood. It cannot mean the height of the buildings, nor of the walls, for neither houses nor walls could be twelve thousand furlongs in height; some think this means the distance from the plain country to the place where the city stood. But what need is there of attempting to determine such measures in such a visionary representation? The quadrangular form intimates its perfection and stability, for the square figure was a figure of perfection among the Greeks; αντρ τετραγωνος, the square or cubical man, was, with them, a man of unsullied integrity, perfect in all things.
entries.e9f990a297349d4e4d564ba3a7be4aa653b9c578: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen56796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56797" type="x-p"/> The wall - a hundred and forty and four cubits - This is twelve, the number of the apostles, multiplied by itself: for twelve times twelve make one hundred and forty-four. <div eID="gen56797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56798" type="x-p"/> The measure of a man, that is, of the angel - The cubit, so called from cubitus, the elbow, is the measure from the tip of the elbow to the tip of the middle finger, and is generally reckoned at one foot and a half, or eighteen inches; though it appears, from some measurements at the pyramids of Egypt, that the cubit was, at least in some cases, twenty-one inches. <div eID="gen56798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56799" type="x-p"/> By the cubit of a man we may here understand the ordinary cubit, and that this was the angel's cubit who appeared in the form of a man. Or suppose we understand the height of the man as being here intended, and that this was the length of the measuring rod. Now allowing this height and rod to be six feet, and that this was intended to have some kind of symbolical reference to the twelve tribes, mentioned <reference osisRef="Rev.21.12">Rev 21:12</reference>, represented by the twelve gates; and to the twelve apostles, represented by the twelve thresholds or foundations; then twenty-four, the number of the tribes and apostles, multiplied by six, make precisely the number one hundred and forty-four.
entries.b92a749c0dd3d2b1dd19a7b043a3d0b126fd1121: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen56799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56800" type="x-p"/> The building of the wall of it was of jasper - The oriental jasper is exceedingly hard, and almost indestructible. Pillars made of this stone have lasted some thousands of years, and appear to have suffered scarcely any thing from the tooth of time. <div eID="gen56800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen56801" type="x-p"/> Pure gold, like unto clear glass - Does not this imply that the walls were made of some beautifully bright yellow stone, very highly polished? This description has been most injudiciously applied to heaven; and in some public discourses, for the comfort and edification of the pious, we hear of heaven with its golden walls, golden pavements, gates of pearl, etc., etc., not considering that nothing of this description was ever intended to be literally understood; and that gold and jewels can have no place in the spiritual and eternal world. But do not such descriptions as these tend to keep up a fondness for gold and ornaments?
